Discovering Makhubela’s World

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We follow the inspiring journey of Dr. Tebogo Makhubela — from his humble beginnings in Soweto to his groundbreaking work in palaeosciences, his story is one of passion, perseverance, and purpose.

Unique Selling Point:
The piece will explore how he defied societal expectations, turned down a conventional mining career, and instead chose to dig into the deeper history of humankind. It is a celebration of African excellence, representation in science, and the power of opportunity when met with talent.


Summary:
The story will be structured around the following six key themes:

His Early Life and Roots
Growing up in Soweto, being the first in his family to attend university, and the early signs of his scientific curiosity.
The Beginning of His Journey
A look at his school days, first science projects, and pivotal moments that set him on the path toward human origins research.
His University Life
Navigating an underrepresented field, rising through academic ranks, and overcoming the barriers of race, class, and access in South Africa’s scientific institutions.
The Wayfinder Award and What It Means
Understanding the significance of the National Geographic Wayfinder title—why it matters to Dr. Makhubela, to the field, and to South Africa as a whole.
His Projects: Rising Star Cave and Homo naledi
An inside look at his contributions to one of the most important palaeoanthropological sites in the world, working alongside leading scientists like Prof. Lee Berger.
Legacy and Inspiration
The impact Dr. Makhubela hopes to leave, his role as a role model for future African scientists, and his vision for science accessibility and transformation.

Press Release:


The Prince of Science
From humble beginnings in Soweto to groundbreaking work in paleo-sciences: Dr. Tebogo Makhubela’s journey is one of passion, perseverance, and purpose. He turned down a conventional mining career, choosing instead to delve into the history of humankind, and helping to clarify and detail our evolutionary timeline. Now, he’s been recognised on the international stage. It’s a story of African excellence, representation in science, and the power of talent when it meets opportunity.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


(Claire) These dark caves with rock formations millions of years old, hold secrets to the origins of humanity.


(Tebogo) They're like a photograph of the Earth once upon a time, before we were even here.


(Claire) Shining a light on the rock's surface reveals how our ancestors once lived.


(Tebogo) Amazing stories about who we are. You know, about our world before our time.


(Claire) Our guide into this ancient burial ground in the cradle of humankind is Dr Tebogo Makhubela, who transformed adversity into purpose and darkness into discovery.


(Upsound MC) Please welcome Tebogo Makhubela, a South African geologist and speleologist.


(Claire) Every year, the prestigious National Geographic Society celebrates the Wayfinder awards, honoring outstanding scientists from all over the world for their contributions to science, conservation and storytelling.


(Tebogo) And that's where I come in, with help from a newly discovered site called Lefika la Noka. I came up with that name.


(Claire) Tebogo was among this year's fifteen global recipients honored for changing how we see our past and our future.


(Tebogo) Lefika la Noka is about to unlock the world of Homo Naledi for everyone, and it captures a record of the past during a time when Homo Naledi was roaming in the Cradle of Humankind World Heritage Site.


(Claire) The cradle of humankind, about 50 kilometers from Johannesburg, is considered the holy grail in the study of human evolution, yielding more early human fossils than any other place on earth. For eleven years, Tebogo has explored these caves as a geologist and speleologist, uncovering how environmental and climate changes have shaped human evolution.


(Tebogo) Every morning I arrive. I get here around seven, because usually we start at eight working and then I walk up.


(Claire) Today, we're heading to the rising star cave, close to where scientists found Homo Naledi, an ancient human relative who lived about three hundred thousand years ago.


(Tebogo) So this will be your helmet for the day.


(Claire) Right?


(Tebogo) Let's try and get it fitted.


(Claire) Striking color. Thank you so much. Oh, can you help me with that?


(Tebogo) Okay, yes. Okay. Is it too tight?


(Claire) It's good.


(Tebogo) Okay.


(Claire) Do I look cute, though?


(Tebogo) Yeah.


(Claire) Okay cool.


(Tebogo) You do. No seriously!


(Claire) Okay. Where are we going?


(Tebogo) We're going down here. There'll be no rope today.


(Claire) Why does the ground ends very fast here?


(Tebogo) So we're gonna take it slow. There is some nice steps. Please be careful. Here. It's stable, but you know, just make sure you don't get your leg inside.


(Claire) Got you. Wow! So you spend your days in these cold, dark places.


(Tebogo) Yes, this is home.


(Claire) Wow!


(Tebogo) Our ancestors are here, so we like to spend time with them here.


(Claire) Wow!


(Claire) Rising Star is undeniably special, as is the importance of the work being done to unravel its secrets.


(Claire) That's amazing. I don't even know what I'm seeing, but I'm impressed.

(tebogo) This is what they were mining in the late 1800s and the early 1900s all the way up until like the 1940s and 1950s. So this we call calcium carbonate. There are rocks formed inside the cave. So they are called Spilliotherms.


(Claire) Spilliotherms.


(Tebogo) Yes


(Claire) Here, deep under the surface. Tebogo's work has shed light on our human history. His research has provided evidence that Homo naledi buried. Their dead, perhaps the oldest of its kind, and by accurately dating these rocks, he's helped to clarify our evolutionary timeline.


(Claire) Do you know what I find so exciting about this story is that Tebogo is a young man from a disadvantaged community talking about geology with such passion and enthusiasm. It's infectious because even I can understand why he loves this work and why it's so important for you and I to understand.


(Claire) Dirk Lambert van royen has worked with Tebogo for over a decade.


(Dirk) His passion is contagious, in a sense, because he's always, you know, he's he loves talking about his his work and and then the whole team gets swept up in the moment.


(Claire) On the surface, more to uncover.


(Claire) I'm seeing lots of rock formations. What's the significance of what I'm seeing here on the ground?


(Tebogo) Sure. So what we have here actually, believe it or not, we're inside a cave.


(Claire) No, we're not.


(Tebogo) Well, so what we're seeing here, it's an outline of the cave, right? The Cave were just in.


(Claire) Ah.


(Tebogo) Yes, so we drew out that cave and then we build it up here on surface. This is like, you know, a factory. So there's a couple of stations, different teams doing different things. We've discovered ways of actually assembling the context again.


(Claire) In other words, this is a rough replica of the world below a kind of above-ground-rock-laboratory. Tebogo's achievements haven't come easily. They followed years of determination from humble beginnings.


(Claire) It all began here in Soweto, where the young de Bucha would be shaped into the man he would become the challenges he faced, like overcrowded classrooms and limited resources at school, and just the daily strife of coming from a poor family. That prepared him for the wider world that lay ahead.


(Claire) In the heart of Soweto, Tebogo's journey began guided by a grandmother who'd nurtured his wonder and love for the Earth.


(Tebogo) She was burning coal, and I was wondering, why are you burning only this type of rocks and not the others? Because there were rocks around in that memory, and she was like, no, no, only certain types of rocks burn.


(Claire) From that moment, Tebogo's love affair with rocks and their hidden stories began lasting well beyond his high school years at the Vuwani secondary school in Chiawelo.


(Claire) We're sitting at your former school. What does it feel like to be here?


(Tebogo) This is where I found myself. A young scholar in me. So it feels great to come back here, because most of my teachers have retired, but there's a few who are still here, so it's good to see them. And I was discussing my research with them, and they were excited. They know Homo Naledi so it feels great.


(Mashudu) He was always having a book with him. Imagine a grade eight learner reading, not just studying, but reading books.


(Claire) Tebogo's Former teacher Mashudu Vhuluahani was especially impressed by this eager student, and worked hard to expose him to a world beyond the classroom.


(Mashudu) I said, if you want to know what success is, let's go, I'll drive and I took them to UJ.


(Claire) Tebogo's matric results earned him a place at the University of Johannesburg, where he first chose to study engineering.


(Tebogo) But at the 11th Hour when I was supposed to register for engineering at UJ, I just ended up registering for geology. Put myself, of course, in serious trouble because I had no funding for geology. I had no bursary.


(Claire) Government support covered tuition and books, but not his food or transport.


(Tebogo) By then, I couldn't even afford the Metro Bus, you know, so I would walk to the station from home. But the tough one was from the Laanglagte station to get to UJ Auckland Park, Kingsway campus. My goodness, that is almost three kilometer one way.


(Claire) By 2019, he'd achieved a PhD, and today, as a Wayfinder award winner, he's shaping minds and changing how we understand our past. To those familiar with Tebogo's determination and work ethic, his success is no surprise.


(dirk) He deserves this award. He's been working very hard for many years, and he's so passionate about everything he does. So I'm very proud.


(Mashudu) That's why I lack words to express myself. I'm delighted honestly. I'm not even surprised. He's still going far. From humble beginnings, from a very, very poor background, but very intelligent and very rich in mind.


(Claire) From a boy making the most of life with his grandmother in Soweto to a scientist studying the beginning of humanity. Tebogo's story is one of curiosity, resilience and hope.


(Tebogo) I'm experiencing my life change, you know, professionally, in ways that I never imagined, whereby I just woke up now I'm the Prince of Science,


(Claire) Yes you are!


(Tebogo) Indeed I am and I appreciate that.
